summary.text: Bird sounds divide into songs, which are longer and more complex and linked to territory and courtship, and calls, which handle jobs like alarms and flock contact.
Birds make song with the syrinx, a bony organ at the bottom of the windpipe, and can control its two sides independently to sound two notes at once.
Song has two main jobs: attracting mates, where its quality may signal fitness, and defending territory, where it can help rivals settle boundaries without a fight.

facts.label: Vocal organ
facts.value: The syrinx, at the bottom of the trachea

facts.label: Duet calls
facts.value: Over 400 bird species engage in them

facts.label: Pitch control
facts.value: Membrane tension sets pitch; exhalation force sets volume

facts.label: Non-vocal sound
facts.value: Bill, wing, tail, feet or feathers make sounds, called sonation

items.prompt: A short, simple cry makes a whole flock scatter when a predator appears. What kind of vocalization is it most likely?

options.label: A song, because songs are the main way birds warn others
A syrinx note, which is neither song nor call
A call, since calls tend to give alarms
A sonation, since warnings use wings or feet

items.explain: Songs are longer and more complex and tied to territory and courtship, while calls tend to serve such functions as alarms or keeping a flock in contact.

items.prompt: A single bird sings two different notes at the same instant. How can its body do that?

options.label: Its vocal organ lets it control each side of the windpipe separately
It has two separate voice boxes at the top of the windpipe
It breathes out and in at once while singing
It switches notes faster than the ear can follow

items.explain: The syrinx sits at the bottom of the trachea, and a bird can control the two sides of the trachea independently, which is how some species produce two notes at once.

items.prompt: In many species, females favour males with bigger song repertoires. What makes that a sensible choice?

options.label: A bigger repertoire shows he has a larger syrinx
A bigger repertoire proves he hatched earlier
More songs keep predators away from the nest
Song quality and repertoire size can signal how fit a male is

items.explain: Song quality may be a good indicator of fitness, and the repertoire also appears to indicate fitness in some species, so a female may choose on those grounds.

items.prompt: Two territorial males trade songs along their boundary, then each stays on his own side. What does the singing do for them?

options.label: It tells each where the other's nest is so he can raid it
It lets each judge the other's quality and avoid a costly fight
It proves both are the same age, ending the dispute
It swaps food between them as a peace offering

items.explain: Territorial birds use song to negotiate boundaries, and because song may be a reliable indicator of quality, rivals can discern each other and prevent an energetically costly fight.

items.prompt: In arid parts of Australia and Africa, females sing as much as males, unlike in northern Eurasia. What explanation is given?

options.label: Males there lack a syrinx and so cannot sing at all
Seasons are so regular that the males sing much less
Birds breed whenever conditions allow, and duets ready both sexes to breed
Few predators live there, which makes singing safe for all

items.explain: Irregular, aseasonal breeding means both sexes must be brought into breeding condition, and vocalization, especially duetting, serves this purpose.

items.prompt: Male manakins can make sounds with body parts rather than the syrinx. What is that kind of sound-making called?

options.label: Duetting
Sonation
Song-type matching
Repertoire matching

items.explain: Producing non-vocal sounds that are intentionally modulated communicative signals, using the bill, wings, tail, feet and body feathers, is called sonation.
